feedback: If a learner expects to watch a single star age, remind them each stage lasts millions to billions of years; astronomers piece the cycle together from many stars at different stages.
If a learner confuses a nebula with a galaxy, clarify: a nebula is a cloud of gas and dust where stars form; a galaxy is a vast collection of stars.
Link the Sun image to prior learning that it is an ordinary main-sequence star.
activities.intendedInsight: The abstract timescales become tangible and awe-inspiring through real images, and we infer the cycle from many stars caught at different stages rather than watching one.
learnerActions: View real imagery of a star nursery nebula (e.g. the Orion Nebula), the Sun as an ordinary main-sequence star, and a supernova remnant.
Optionally take a fly-through of a nebula or a supernova set-piece as a wonder moment.
Match each image to its place on the life-cycle story you learned.
Discuss why we never watch one star change: stages take millions to billions of years, so we see many stars at different stages — like photographing a forest to infer one tree's life.
activities.title: Awe imagery of birth and death

feedback: If a learner orders the stages wrongly, replay the diagram walkthrough and retry.
If a learner picks 'size/brightness' over mass, restate that mass is the property that decides both lifespan and ending.
If a learner says the massive star lasts longer, explain it burns its larger fuel supply far faster and hotter, so it lasts only a few million years while the Sun shines for billions.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can recall and apply the stage order and its branch, name mass as the deciding property, and recognise that massive stars live shortest.
learnerActions: Put the life stages in order with the branch intact: nebula → main-sequence star → then either (low mass) giant → white dwarf, or (high mass) supergiant → supernova.
Answer: 'What single property decides whether a star becomes a white dwarf or a supernova?' (its mass).
Match each mass (small / massive) to its ending (white dwarf / supernova).
Answer the surprise puzzle: which lasts longer, a huge massive star or a small one like the Sun — and why?
activities.title: Check the sequence and the branch
